We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to solve a system of monotone inclusion problems. This method can be broken down into the combination of the proximal forward-backward algorithm and an extrapolation step. It possesses three key properties: it globally converges to a solution regardless of its initial choice, uses proximal distances that can be flexible and arbitrary, and has a locally convergent rate when proximal distances are fixed. Moreover, we provide a criterion for selecting suitable distances and demonstrate that, with specific distances, DWIFOB reduces to the extrapolated forward-backward algorithm. This method also possesses the same properties as the latter. Finally, we illustrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments. Federated Learning is an innovative approach to collaborative machine learning that balances data privacy and performance. It enables multiple clients to jointly train a single model without compromising their sensitive data, by doing so in a decentralized manner. However, the communication limitations of FL often lead to subpar convergence and a less accurate model. To address this issue, researchers have recently introduced Federated Distillation, a technique that transcends the communication constraints by transmitting aggregated student and teacher model outputs. While FD achieves better communication efficiency, it also results in a less interpretable model. To mitigate this, we introduce Communication-Efficient Federated Distillation, a modification of FD that reduces communication costs without compromising performance. Our method is built upon two key ideas: first, we substitute FD's base line output aggregation with a more compact representation; second, we introduce a novel distillation method that significantly reduces communication costs. Our experimental results demonstrate that CEFED outperforms FD and achieves state-of-the-art performance under communication-constrained settings. Moreover, CEFED's improvements are accompanied by enhanced model transparency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuc/CEFED. In risk-sensitive reinforcement learning, the objective is to maximize the exponential return of a Markov decision process under a finite horizon. Our research focuses on non-stationary environments where policies become suboptimal over time. We introduce a new dynamic regret measure for risk-sensitive reinforcement learning, which yields near-optimal results with a logarithmic rate of change. To achieve this, we developed an algorithm that combines an adaptive detection method for identifying changes and a policy optimization technique that separates risk-sensitive value function estimation. Our dynamic regret analysis is the first to achieve logarithmic regret in non-stationary risk-sensitive reinforcement learning. We also demonstrated that existing approaches have a much worse regret of at least quadratic in the number of changes. Experiment results validate our algorithm's efficiency and adaptability. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhongyuan-liu/RS-NonStationary-RL.

This approach allows our agent to successfully track the obstacle in complex 3D environments. Binary matrix datasets are common in various disciplines, and researchers often require analyzing large numbers of such matrices. These datasets typically exhibit a fixed margin, signifying that the sum of each row and column is constant and known in advance. This fixed margin constraint significantly reduces the total number of possible matrices. To facilitate analysis, uniformly sampling binary matrices at fixed margins can provide valuable insights; however, this task is computationally challenging. This study presents an efficient algorithm for non-uniform sampling of binary matrices based on a given distribution specified by a probability vector. The proposed algorithm can sample matrices of any size in O(n^2 log^2 n) time, where n represents the number of rows (or columns). The algorithm's underlying technique involves transforming the sampling problem into selecting a random path in a directed acyclic graph. The study also offers precomputed inverse covariance binomial distributions for small sizes, enabling rapid extension to larger datasets. The algorithm's practical efficiency is demonstrated through a range of experiments. Additionally, the study shares sampling binary matrices at fixed columns, a problem that had gone unsolved. The study's implementation is available online.

Quantization has been proven to be beneficial in reducing the computational cost and memory requirements of neural networks at inference time. This study aims to provide a deeper understanding of the effect of quantization on generalization performance. We demonstrate that binary weight quantization can be viewed as a regularization technique that restricts the neural tangent kernel, and this kernel's spectrum plays a crucial role in determining the generalization performance. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the quantization error and the generalization performance by analyzing the eigenvalues of the neural tangent kernel. This analysis enables the estimation of the required quantization error for achieving a specified generalization performance. Additionally, we introduce a novel training method that combines binary weight quantization with an optimized quantization error, and this approach achieves superior results when applied to various convolutional neural networks. Our source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyu-1994/BinaryNN.

We have developed a universal method to calculate the crossing multipliers for solvable lattice models using the algebraic and conformal properties inherent to these systems. By applying this method, we have derived exact expressions for the crossing multipliers of the critical isotropic 3D lattice models and the associated W-algebras. Furthermore, we have used these multipliers to calculate the long-distance asymptotic behavior of the 3D critical isotropic ferromagnetic model's correlation functions. Additionally, we have determined the asymptotic properties of the 4-point conformal block in 3D systems. Our proposed method can be extended to other solvable lattice models possessing similar algebraic structures. Such models include the 3D + 1 quantum Yang-Mills systems and the 3D systems with a Griffiths phase. The universal nature of our approach also enables the calculation of asymptotic long-distance behaviors in these systems. The general framework of our method can be found in arXiv:2102.02120.

Capturing the intricate morphology of individual cells from live cell images is a crucial task in cell biology, yet current methods face significant challenges in dealing with the cell's complex shape, limited training data, and variability in cell forms. To address this problem, we propose a new implicit neural representation, which enables us to model cell shapes as a continuous function in three-dimensional space. Our approach, called CellGAN, uses a conditional normalizing flow to generate cell shapes from a conditional vector, and has been demonstrated to effectively capture the morphology of cells, even with a small dataset. CellGAN's performance was evaluated in a controlled environment, and the results show its superiority over existing shape representation methods. Furthermore, we successfully applied CellGAN to generate cell shapes that resemble those found in a real cell imaging dataset. The source code for CellGAN is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhaozh/cellgan.

Researchers in neuroscience hypothesize that the brain encodes spatial information in a specific, consistent framework. This theory suggests that proximity in this framework determines relative importance, with areas closer to each other perceived as more similar. A novel type of reinforcement learning, called intrinsic reinforcement learning, can be represented in a geometry that is similar to the brain's proposed spatial framework. Our findings reveal that this geometric structure is not unique to intrinsic reinforcement learning and can be found in other types of reinforcement learning as well. Moreover, we discovered that the brain's spatial framework is more suitable for representing learning dynamics compared to Euclidean geometry. Ultimately, the geometric structure of the brain's spatial framework may provide a more accurate model for how the brain processes spatial information. This geometric structure could also offer insights for the development of more efficient machine learning algorithms. Additionally, our research may provide valuable insights for neuroscientists seeking to understand the brain's spatial representation. This paper introduces a novel method for sound event localization and detection, employing a convolutional recurrent neural network with rectangular filters. In the presence of significant inertial effects, vibrations within a classical background can induce substantial dynamic correlations between electrons, spins, and the lattice. These correlations are substantial when the characteristic frequencies of the lattice and the relevant electronic or magnetic parameters align. A model demonstrating the creation of a topological insulating phase through inertial spin-phonon interactions is presented, with the added capacity of controlling phase boundaries through phonon frequency. Furthermore, the induced dynamic electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions can lead to the generation of quantized currents and magnetic fields. A generalized Mott transition is also described, with the lower and upper Mott gaps separated by a gapless state induced by the dynamic spin-phonon interactions. Finally, the possibility of achieving stable static solitons in one-dimensional systems with dynamic spin-phonon interactions is explored. These solitons can serve as stable outlets for the extra charge and magnetic flux. A potential experimental realization of this phenomenon is also proposed.

This paper introduces a visual relocalization approach that utilizes a geometrically accurate 3D surfel map generated from prior experiences. To achieve this, we combine a state-of-the-art surfel creation method with a novel descriptor learning framework designed to produce more distinctive and generalizable features. By leveraging a pre-built surfel map, our approach significantly enhances the relocalization success rate, particularly in challenging scenarios with limited training data. To further optimize performance, we developed an efficient matching strategy that reduces computational costs and improves accuracy within the map. To validate our method, we conducted extensive experiments on the KITTI dataset, achieving a 76.19% relocalization rate with a SurfNet-trained descriptor. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art surfel-based localizers by 10.1% and 5.5% in the synthetic and real-world datasets, respectively. Our code and dataset are available for public access at https://github.com/zhengyuli2019/sufel_map.

The framework's lower bound is established, and empirical results demonstrate that our approach accelerates convergence and yields better performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Current pseudo-labeling approaches for enhancing the performance of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) rely on naive strategies for selecting pseudo-targets, often choosing random unlabelled graph nodes to supplement training data. In an attempt to improve upon this method, we've developed a more effective pseudo-labeling technique that prioritizes informative unlabelled graph nodes with unique features. Our approach, Informed Pseudo-Labeling for GNNs (IPL-GNN), involves evaluating candidate nodes based on their local neighbourhood structures to determine the most discriminative pseudo-targets. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing pseudo-labeling techniques for GNNs. Furthermore, we've successfully integrated IPL-GNN with two prominent GNN architectures, revealing its potential to improve model accuracy and serve as a general framework for future research. We investigate the behavior of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on smooth and strongly-convex functions with Gaussian data, analyzing its average-case performance relative to its optimal outcome. Our findings demonstrate that: (1) SGD achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}\left( \log(T) / N \right)$, with $T$ denoting the number of iterations; (2) this rate is both robust to non-symmetric data and universally applicable to a broad class of functions; (3) the same convergence rate applies to a diverse set of strongly-convex functions, including those with non-convex lower-bounds, as long as the data has thin tails; (4) we also establish a sharp threshold for tail-matter, dictating whether or not our average-case analysis yields a superior convergence rate compared to the classical worst-case scenario. Our research provides a precise understanding of the trade-off between average-case performance and robustness to data asymmetry. Moreover, it highlights the significance of tail-matter in optimizing SGD's average-case behavior. Lastly, it opens up new avenues for investigating the performance of SGD in the convex regime. The widespread adoption of AI systems in high-stakes settings poses significant risks to individuals and society if these systems fail. To mitigate these dangers, it is crucial to learn from past AI failures and near-misses. Currently, there is no centralized database documenting AI incidents. We propose creating the AI Incident Database (AIDb), an open-source resource gathering and standardizing reports of AI system failures. The AIDb will facilitate in-depth analysis of global AI incident trends and serve as a knowledge base for preventing future failures. We outline the initial framework and database structure for the AIDb, as well as the methodology for collecting and evaluating incident reports. We also present preliminary findings on the current state of AI incidents. We hope the AIDb will become a valuable tool for the AI community, enabling us to learn from our past and build safer AI systems for the future. We invite readers to contribute to the AIDb by submitting incident reports at https://aidb.org/.

Finally, we outline promising directions for future research in process prescriptive monitoring.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation often employs pre-training with a classification task to save time and improve performance. However, this approach may not be optimal if we utilize unlabeled data for self-supervised learning of image representation through a segmentation task. In this research, we evaluate whether depth estimation, a well-established self-supervised learning method, can serve as a more effective pre-training technique than classification for semantic segmentation. We introduce a novel, efficient depth estimation approach based on a volume rendering loss function and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods. Our experimental results confirm that depth estimation provides superior pre-training performance compared to classification, and we achieve state-of-the-art performance on Pascal Context and ADE20K datasets. In various applications like software logging, sensor records, and security alerts, large volumes of time-stamped data are generated. These sequences are often described using basic events like "CPU usage exceeded 90% at time t". Existing text generation methods are not well-suited for creating coherent and informative narratives from such data. To address this, we introduce TCube, a novel neural framework that can summarize time-series data in a wide range of domains. TCube employs a dual transformer architecture, where the first transformer predicts event timestamps, and the second generates the corresponding descriptions. We also propose a new evaluation metric, called Temporal Narrative Coherence, to assess the plausibility of generated narratives. Our experiments demonstrate that TCube surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art sequence-to-sequence models and a range of domain-specific and neural approaches. Notably, TCube achieves a 0.64 F1 score in the high-precision category of the Time Series Narration Challenge 2022, outperforming the runner-up by 0.35 in that category. TCube's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepMind/TCube.

The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered a significant surge in online rumors across China, which have the potential to cause severe harm to public health. To address this issue, we have developed an innovative framework for measuring the influence of rumors and detecting their propagation channels. Our framework combines the Kullback-Leibler divergence with local spreading probabilities to identify high-impact rumors. Furthermore, we have refined the traditional rumor spreading model by introducing a memory-based diffusion mechanism, which accurately represents Chinese online rumor dissemination. By applying our framework to the Sina Weibo platform, we have obtained valuable insights into rumor propagation and demonstrated the effectiveness of our methods in a real-world setting. Moreover, we have explored the relationship between rumor influence and user behavior. Our results show that the peak influence of rumors is typically reached within one to three days of initial detection. Additionally, we have found that most rumors are propagated by a small proportion of highly active users. Our study provides quantitative analysis and spreads analysis to aid authorities in understanding online rumor propagation and inform strategies for rumor detection and dissemination control. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/chenyong1206/COVID-19_Rumor.

Our method utilizes a class of neural networks, known as linear models, to reproduce the original high-accuracy network's outputs. By iteratively replacing a portion of the original network's non-linear components with their linear counterparts, we achieve substantial reductions in size and computational requirements while maintaining high overall accuracy. Our experiments show that this compression approach outperforms existing methods for sentiment analysis and question-answering tasks, and we also provide a mathematical explanation for its success. Furthermore, we showcase the applicability of this compression technique to other types of neural networks and diverse tasks. Reinforcement learning models often rely on historical data for pretraining, but their performance can be compromised if the data is contaminated with biased examples. Current methods for learning from incomplete data are vulnerable to performance degradation in the presence of corrupted data. We present a new framework for robust reinforcement learning that can handle a variety of data corruption. Our approach involves maximizing the minimum return that can be achieved when removing a certain number of corrupted examples. We also provide a tractable reformulation of this problem and propose an efficient algorithm based on convex optimization. We evaluate our method on a range of challenging tasks and find that it significantly outperforms existing models by withstanding a high level of corruption without a substantial decline in performance. We further demonstrate that our method can be extended to handle more severe forms of corruption and perform better under such conditions. Our code is available online at https://github.com/alexandre-garivier/crobol.

now possible to analyze openings quantitatively and uncover their intricate

distinct groups. Our research also demonstrates that chess openings are diverse 
in their patterns of move sequences and that players' preferences for different 
openings are correlated with their levels of skill. Furthermore, we have 
developed a new metric to measure the complexity of chess openings, and our data 
shows that more advanced players tend to prefer complex openings. Our work has 
implications for chess instruction and can be used to inform future research in

The study involves identifying the possible twists and their corresponding representations, given that the order of the twist must divide the volume of the torus. The results show that these twisted torus coverings provide numerous examples of non-productive, orientable, relativistic spacetimes with a torus topology, along with non-trivial, crystallographically-symmetric spacetimes. The study also offers a representation of the crystallographic point groups in the twisted torus scenario, which is distinct from the standard representation. The results will be presented in 3D Bolzano Prize Seminar.

Our research introduces a significant enhancement to these models by replacing the original generator with a VQGAN, thereby substantially improving low-frequency painting quality and reducing high-frequency noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability of these models to paint on arbitrary dimensions, achieving novel 3D and spherical painting generation. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a complex neurological condition characterized by excessive hyperactivity, inattention, and impulsivity. Recent advances in neuroimaging technology have enabled researchers to identify distinct patterns of brain activity that differentiate ADHD patients from healthy individuals. This study aims to improve ADHD diagnosis by pinpointing the essential components of the brain involved in this disorder. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data from the OpenNeuro repository to identify the critical regions that distinguish ADHD patients from controls. This was achieved through a systematic evaluation of various brain regions using a deep learning model. Our results show that focusing on a specific subset of regions can enhance ADHD diagnosis, with the optimal configuration comprising regions including the cerebellum, frontal areas, parietal regions, and temporal lobes. This finding enables the development of a location-aware model, which significantly outperformed existing models by delivering an accuracy of 87.5%, 83.3%, and 80.6% in classifying ADHD, control, and mixed samples respectively. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of data standardization and data augmentation in deep learning-based ADHD diagnosis. We also demonstrate that our model can accurately identify ADHD patients based on functional brain activity patterns. This study's findings contribute to a deeper understanding of ADHD's neural basis and provide valuable insights for developing diagnostic systems using neuroimaging data. With its high accuracy, our model has the potential to be used in clinical settings for ADHD diagnosis. The code and data used in this study are available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. Acronyms are commonly used in everyday language, with three or four letter abbreviations for words or organizations, and sometimes longer expansions. They can be found in various domains such as medicine, law, and business. Although acronyms may seem straightforward, they often require clarification due to multiple possible interpretations. In this research, we introduce MadDog, a web-based system designed to identify and resolve acronym ambiguities. MadDog utilizes a data-driven approach, drawing from the Wiktionary database to suggest possible definitions for acronyms. Users can then select relevant definitions, which are subsequently ranked and displayed to aid in disambiguation. MadDog offers a user-friendly interface and supports offline access. We evaluate the system's performance using two datasets and provide a comparison with BERT, a leading language model. We also highlight the system's capabilities through two practical case studies. MadDog is currently accessible at https://madog.acronyms/.

The rapid growth in data is overwhelming current storage capacity, prompting exploration into DNA data storage as a potential solution due to its exceptionally high data density. We investigate enhancing the efficiency of DNA data storage by leveraging base pairs in DNA that can exist in two distinct states, denoting bits in a binary code. We present a new data structure called the ordered multi-base tree, which effectively supports data updates and hierarchy queries within this binary code. We demonstrate that this data structure offers improved read and write efficiency compared to existing approaches, with the added benefit of reducing storage costs by minimizing the number of distinct DNA constructs required. We validate our design through comprehensive simulations, which show significant enhancements in read and write performance as well as storage efficiency. Specifically, our results indicate a 3.6 to 8 times increase in read rate, a 3 to 6 times decrease in write operations, and up to 3.6 times better storage efficiency. We also show that our data structure can be adapted for use in traditional binary DNA storage with comparable performance. Furthermore, we propose a novel method for efficiently encoding large hierarchies into DNA, which significantly reduces storage costs by a factor of up to 3.6 with minimal DNA construct complexity. Notably, it surpasses the performance of a strong question answering model that has been trained on labeled data, indicating its effectiveness in new intent discovery. The framework's source code will be made available.

To address the data sparsity issue affecting session-based recommendation models, we've developed a self-supervised graph co-training framework. This method utilizes an internal data augmentation procedure to produce a comprehensive graph from session data, which is then split into two parts for co-training. One half of the data is used to derive node representations through self-supervised learning, while the other half is used for supervised learning. These two models are trained in an alternating manner until convergence. We've tested our approach on two real-world datasets and achieved notable improvements over state-of-the-art session-based recommendation models. Notably, our method outperforms existing self-supervised and supervised graph models by 2.0% and 1.3% respectively in terms of AUC. This self-supervised graph co-training framework offers a versatile approach to addressing data sparsity issues. Its code will be made publicly available.

This research presents a hybrid approach to word prediction that integrates the Naive Bayes and Hidden Information models. The Naive Bayes model is initially applied to estimate the likelihood of a word given its prefix, while the Hidden Information model is utilized to determine the probability of a word given its context through latent information. A word is then selected by combining these two probabilities in the form of a Naive Bayes-Hidden Information model. Experiments were conducted to evaluate this hybrid model, comparing its performance to the Naive Bayes and Hidden Information models. Notably, the hybrid model outperformed the Naive Bayes model and demonstrated comparable results with the Hidden Information model. Furthermore, the model's capacity to capture latent information using Naive Bayes was investigated. We investigate the dynamics of active colloidal dimers in activity gradients, focusing on their behavior when active components are confined to a single rod or when dimers are attached to a surface with an activity gradient. This behavior is influenced by the active strength of the colloid and the distance between the active parts. This research also reveals that these dimers can create self-organizing structures, such as circular arrays, in the parameter space that defines their collective motion. Moreover, we found that these dimers can transition between rotating and stationary states in response to changes in the active strength or their spatial arrangement. Wikipedia's reliance on volunteer editors has led to a significant issue: approximately 10% of articles are of poor quality due to inadequate editing. Wikipedia's lack of a reliable quality control system makes it challenging to identify and address these poor quality articles. This research aims to improve the efficiency of Wikipedia's quality control by developing an automated system that identifies and labels poor quality articles using editing behaviors and their relationships with article quality. This system was trained on a large dataset of articles and human editors, as well as changes made to those articles, allowing it to predict article quality with 60% accuracy. When compared to existing Wikipedia quality control processes, this automated system reduced the number of articles requiring human review by 30%. Additionally, this study found that Wikipedia's editing behaviors contain more detailed information about article quality than the articles themselves, highlighting the importance of considering the behaviors of human editors in understanding complex systems. This research has the potential to be applied to other crowdsourced projects that rely on volunteer contributions. This paper will be presented at IJCAI 2023. It offers a more accessible alternative to traditional knowledge distillation and can serve as a standalone model transfer technique. Imitation learning is a crucial technique for developing agent policies by emulating expert behavior. However, obtaining high-quality expert demonstrations is often challenging and expensive due to the requirement for extensive data collection. In this research, we introduce a novel framework called Co-Imitation Learning that enables agents to learn from the behavior of peers that serve as experts. The method leverages a joint loss function to optimize both the imitator and the peer expert, resulting in improved performance and more efficient learning. The framework's benefits were demonstrated through successful applications in diverse environments, including classic control problems and half-cheetah gait restoration. The code is publicly accessible on https://github.com/robot-learning/co-imitation-learning.

PAC codes are a type of error-correcting codes that can efficiently correct random errors, and they have been shown to be computationally efficient and capable of large code distances. However, calculating the error metric of PAC codes is a complex task, and we present a simplified approach to compute this metric, which allows us to determine upper and lower bounds on the minimum error probability of these codes. By applying this new metric, we are ableto assess the performance of PAC codes on various channels and provide a method to optimize their decoding algorithms. The growing availability of data and computational resources has led to a significant shift from traditional, physically-based modeling to data-driven approaches in engineering and science. While data-driven models often exhibit superior performance in specific contexts, they frequently lack physical underpinnings and can be challenging to interpret. Furthermore, data-driven models may not be suitable for tasks outside their original scope of application. In this paper, we explore the potential of cooperative modeling, which integrates data-driven and physically-based models to leverage the strengths of both approaches. A cooperative model of this nature can provide a more comprehensive understanding of a system by combining the benefits of data-driven and physically-based modeling, even if the data is limited or biased. We illustrate the principles of cooperative modeling by developing a simplified example of a Rijke tube, which is a classic system for studying premixed combustion. We then compare the performance of various modeling methodologies, including data-driven, physically-based, and cooperative approaches, to demonstrate their potential to address different research questions. The results of our study suggest that cooperative modeling offers a promising framework for tackling complex problems at the intersection of physics and data analytics. This approach can facilitate a deeper understanding of a system by integrating the insights of both physically-based and data-driven models. In addition to providing improved accuracy and physical plausibility, cooperative models may also enable the transfer of knowledge across different data conditions and applications. We envision cooperative modeling to be a versatile tool that can be utilized in a wide range of domains, including but not limited to combustion research. The underlying methodology of cooperative modeling can be adapted to various fields of study and we anticipate it to be a valuable asset in the realm of data science and physics-informed machine learning. The study also explores the impact of different channel models on degree-degree correlation and discovers that the binary erasure channel tends to produce LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlation more frequently than other models. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm through numerical experiments in various machine learning applications. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Chen-YuCheng/DR-DSGD.

This study introduces a groundbreaking approach to estimating object shapes and positions from semantic keypoints in two- and three-dimensional formats. Building on the success of PCL in category-level shape prediction, we develop a robust optimization method that effectively handles noisy keypoints in 2D and 3D formats. We also introduce a new dataset, the Semantic POSEidon, comprising rich annotations for over 100,000 marine containers across various categories, enabling pose and shape estimation. Our method demonstrates superior performance in both 2D and 3D formats, outperforming PCL and other shape estimation models. Furthermore, we highlight the importance of robust optimization in 3D shape estimation, particularly when dealing with keypoint noise. Our code and dataset will be publicly available.

A new method for calculating the required sample size in clinical trials where treatments are assessed across multiple subpopulations is proposed. In trials where patient data is shared across various subgroups, our formula takes into account the degree of information sharing and ensures that each subgroup trial meets predefined criteria for statistical significance. The formula is based on an extension of the Berman-Fine formula for Bayesian trials and assumes equal prior distributions for each subgroup trial. An example demonstrates how to use the formula in practice. Simulation results show that our approach accurately estimates the required sample size when there is limited borrowing of information and tends to underestimate it when there is significant borrowing. Deep learning techniques have greatly improved segmentation capabilities in medical imaging, particularly in MRI and PET images. However, training deep learning models for multi-modal image segmentation requires a substantial amount of annotated data, which can be time-consuming and labor-intensive to obtain. This study introduces an innovative approach to segmenting images from multiple modalities without labeling them, focusing on MRI and PET images as a key use case. We propose the Cyclic Segmentation Gan, a cyclic generative adversarial network architecture that can segment images from multiple modalities in an unsupervised manner. This method is evaluated on a dataset consisting of 20 abdominal MRI and PET scans, achieving a moderate level of accuracy comparable to supervised methods, with segmentation maps of unlabeled PET images showing promising results. This study showcases the potential of unsupervised multi-modal segmentation, which may be an important tool in low-resource settings or when data annotation is challenging. A new approach, Transformation-Specific Smoothing, has been developed to enhance the robustness of these models by utilizing a transformation matrix to filter out noisy data during training and inference. Interestingly, this method can be applied to any regression loss function and is compatible with various models, including the Franklin Network. Experimental results demonstrate that TPC outperforms existing smoothing methods by a significant margin on multiple datasets. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the method's performance under different parameter settings is provided. This method has been successfully integrated into a 3D object detection system, where it has shown substantial improvement in robustness while maintaining comparable accuracy. However, these methods have not been able to effectively capture temporal links.
This paper proposes a new approach that uses a low-rank and model-agnostic
representation method for temporal knowledge graph completion. The proposed
model consists of two main components: a low-rank score model and a model-
agnostic temporal model. The low-rank score model generates high-quality
embeddings for entities and relations, while the model-agnostic temporal model
utilizes a low-rank score space to determine the temporal relationships among
entities. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach
significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on three benchmark datasets.

In sound design, the ground sound effect is frequently overlooked, yet it plays a crucial role in immersive 3D audio experiences by creating a sense of spatiality and perspective. Ground sound is a particular type of sound propagation that has been largely unexplored in existing research. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by examining the impact of ground sound on 3D audio rendering from a computer graphics perspective. We have developed a novel algorithm for ground sound propagation and demonstrated its practical applications in sound design within virtual environments. Our findings indicate that ground sound can significantly influence sound perception and create a more immersive environment. Additionally, we have identified several areas for further research and potential connections to other fields like physics-based rendering and global illumination. Ultimately, this study seeks to inspire more accurate sound rendering techniques that prioritize perceptual accuracy.

Achieving Bell nonlocality requires overcoming two obstacles: creating a entangled state and obtaining correlations greater than random chance. We've developed a new method to perfectly demonstrate Bell nonlocality without using inequalities by leveraging strong, yet imperfect correlations. This technique offers a practical advantage over previous approaches, as it only necessitates preparing a entangled state once, eliminating the need for correlation preparation. We've successfully applied this method in an experiment using two qubits, obtaining strong correlations exceeding 90% without the need for error correction. This experiment serves as a reliable test of Bell nonlocality and quantum entanglement, and its results are available as open-source data. Additionally, our method has theoretical applications for no-cloning theorem scenarios and device-independent quantum key distribution. We've also explored the connection between our results and previous experiments on Bell nonlocality, highlighting our new method's advantages. In flat band systems, constrained environments lead to atypical behaviors, often resulting in complete localization of all wave functions at the origin. This principle has been exploited in the construction of ultra-cold atomic experiments, which we revisit through a generalized mathematical framework applicable to any flat band condition. Our approach allows for the identification of a self-imprisoning potential, which can localize wave functions, and leads to a theorem confirming that complete localization is only achievable in one dimension. Furthermore, we extend the concept of flat bands to position-dependent Hamiltonians, which fail to produce completely localized states. We substantiate our findings with examples of flat bands derived from position-independent Hamiltonians, including a novel model based on a twisted p orbit. Lastly, we outline potential directions for future research involving ultra-cold atomic experiments.

This study introduces an innovative data-driven approach to clustering dynamical systems. Building on recent advancements in system identification, this method utilizes observed data to determine a low-dimensional model representing the dynamics at hand. It then employs a measure of influence among system trajectories to group similar dynamics together. The proposed clustering method is mathematically justified and demonstrated on various examples, including a hybrid smooth and impact dynamic, a spinning top, and a chaotic system with multiple clusters. Additionally, this study showcases its capability to group multiple, diverse dynamics present in a double pendulum on a vibrating support. The developed method is akin to the k-means clustering algorithm but tailored for applications in dynamical systems, and it outperforms a standard data-driven clustering method that doesn't take the dynamic nature of the data into account. Furthermore, this study is accessible to users without extensive background knowledge in dynamical systems. The implementation details are available in the open-source Python package PyDy.

However, we show that a redshift-dependent HI bias can mitigate these distortions, thereby improving the HI power spectrum recovery. Our results indicate that even with optimal HI bias assumptions, foregrounds may still dominate the HI power spectrum at redshifts less than 1.5 and angular scales below ~20-30 degrees. We establish that for a right ideal in a non-commutative Banach algebra, independence implies infinite dimensionality when the algebra is equipped with an non-degenerate, bounded linear form. This dimensionality criterion can be applied to identify right ideals with specific linear forms that are closed under a particular class of operators, including those with bounded inverse weights. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a non-commutative Banach algebra with a bounded linear form, infinite dimensionality does not necessarily imply independence. However, we show that for a specific type of right ideal in such an algebra, infinite dimensionality is equivalent to independence. Additionally, we provide a characterization of right ideals in non-commutative Banach algebras that are closed under bounded linear forms and linear extensions. Finally, we explore connections between independence, dimensionality, and operator properties in non-commutative Banach algebras and provide several illustrative examples. These results build upon previous work by several authors, including Buss and Strauss, who investigated similar problems in commutative Banach algebras. Our findings also address questions and problems proposed by other mathematicians, including Buss and Laustsen. Finally, we present an open problem for further study.

We propose parity-symmetry-protected bundle emission, a phenomenon where multiple photons are emitted simultaneously through a closed quantum system, guaranteed by fundamental symmetry. By incorporating parity conservation, we demonstrate the occurrence of bundle emission in two-dimensional systems, such as in a lattice of four atoms, where all possible multi-photon states become stable and cannot be absorbed. This concept is applicable to various two-dimensional systems with discrete point group symmetries and potentially used for quantum communication, enabling the distribution of multi-photon bundles for secure key distribution. Furthermore, we explore the application of bundle emission to generate Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger entanglement, a triphoton state with quantum correlation that can be achieved through parity protection. Our work opens a new pathway to create and utilize complex multi-photon states, expanding the field of quantum information and communication.

To enhance the efficiency of large language models, we propose a new distillation technique that effectively transfers knowledge from multiple labeled teachers to a single student model. Our approach, called PILE, works by matching the logits of each teacher model with the student model's logits and labels, and iteratively refining these comparisons until convergence. PILE's simple and symmetric design enables it to be easily integrated into existing student model training pipelines, and experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in convergence rate, accuracy, and data efficiency compared to previous methods. The implementation of PILE is available at https://github.com/leodido/PILE.

We investigate the sensitivity of a novel technique, intensity interferometry, in detecting ultralight bosonic dark matter. By analyzing the anisotropic intensity interferometry, we find that it offers significantly better sensitivity compared to conventional measurements. In particular, we demonstrate that it is possible to detect bosonic dark matter with masses between $10^{-22}$ and $10^{-17}$ eV, a range that falls within the fuzzy dark matter boundary. Furthermore, we highlight that future high-power laser facilities, such as MACE or ALFABIT, can enhance our sensitivity by several orders of magnitude. In addition, we discuss how anisotropic intensity interferometry can be improved with multiple beam setups, potentially reaching even lower sensitivity limits. In this improved scenario, we predict that it will be possible to detect bosonic dark matter across an extremely broad range of $10^{-26}$ to $10^{-9}$ eV. A crucial component in fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics is the vector transport equation. Researchers have developed novel, exact finite element methods to solve this equation using the lowest-order Raviart-Thomas elements, achieving high precision but limited applicability due to quadrilateral element restrictions. This study enhances existing approximate methods, allowing them to be used on general quadrilateral meshes, while also surpassing existing high-order methods in accuracy. A thorough error analysis is provided along with confirmatory numerical experiments. Interestingly, the proposed method demonstrates optimal error performance in complex geometries, even when the exact transport operator is not perfectly represented within the finite element framework. This is particularly evident in highly anisotropic quadrilaterals. This study also offers a thorough error analysis for the vector transport equation, filling a significant gap in the existing finite element literature. parameters across multiple GPUs can lead to suboptimal convergence due to

the performance of model-parallel training, achieving comparable end-to-end
convergence to data parallel training on various GPU architectures and large
neural network setups. Furthermore, local critic training offers improved
robustness to communication delays and network bandwidth constraints. The code
is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexmn/local_critic_training.

A monolithic small collection-electrode detector, CLICTD, is being developed as a technical prototype for the LHCb upgrade. This innovative approach was successfully tested on a large laboratory-scale system with 1.5-meter focal length and 60cm aperture, allowing for high-speed low-resolution wavefront sensing. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss, which is becoming more crucial with the growing complexity of computational models and increasing data volumes. To achieve this, researchers have been adapting traditional algorithms to use non-volatile memory, while developing new techniques to ensure system reliability in the event of a crash. This research focuses on a specific class of algorithms known as iterative solvers, which are commonly used to solve complex mathematical equations. To guarantee data integrity, we propose an algorithmic approach to create checkpointing schedules tailored to the specific memory access patterns of each type of iterative solver, allowing for efficient use of non-volatile memory and optimal crash recovery performance. Our results demonstrate that this method can significantly reduce the cost of creating checkpoints, enabling a significant decrease in overall program runtime and the number of checkpoints. This approach also provides a framework for designing checkpointing schedules and analyzing memory access patterns, which can be applied to other types of algorithms as well. Our study includes a detailed evaluation of the performance benefits, which shows that our method can achieve significant speedup in practical scenarios. Specifically, we found that our approach can result in a 20-30% reduction in program runtime. This research provides a foundation for further investigation into algorithmic approaches to creating checkpointing schedules, which can be used to develop more efficient fault-tolerance mechanisms for high-performance computing systems. Suicidal ideation is a critical indicator of potential mental health crises that requires early detection to prevent tragic outcomes.  Recent research has demonstrated that machine learning models can effectively identify suicidal ideation from individual perspectives, yet real-time identification of high-risk individuals demands consideration of multiple data sources.  This study presents a deep sequential model that integrates information from multiple perspectives, including the patient's, to improve suicidal ideation prediction.  The proposed model is validated on a dataset of 1,437 patients comprising 3,062 clinical notes, and outperforms a comparable model that processes notes sequentially by achieving a 6% higher AUC score. Radio map estimation is a crucial process for enhancing wireless networks' performance and reliability. Traditional radio map estimation methods rely on extensive human-based measurements, which can be both time-consuming and costly. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative approach that leverages autonomous UAVs to create high-quality radio maps. By equipping each UAV with a radio frequency (RF)-enabled sensor, we develop a novel optimization framework that maximizes coverage and accurate radio map estimation. Our approach is complemented by a plug-and-play deep learning-based method, which enables accurate radio map prediction using only a few UAV measurements. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed solutions, showcasing improved radio map estimation and reduced prediction error. Notably, our deep learning-based method exhibits exceptional generalization capabilities, achieving a 90% reduction in inference time and outperforming the baseline estimation method with a prediction error decrease of up to 60%. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu/AerialRM.

This paper introduces a novel unsupervised anomaly detection technique, called Gauge Likelihood Analysis (GLA), which integrates Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and clustering methods. The parameters of this model are refined using the Baum-Welch algorithm, and its likelihoods are calculated through the Forward algorithm. These likelihoods are clustered, and an anomaly region is identified based on the clustering results. The effectiveness of GLA is demonstrated in a real-world industrial control system (ICS) anomaly detection scenario. The study compares GLA to two alternative methods: a supervised detector and an unsupervised detector based on autoencoders. The evaluation shows that GLA outperforms these methods in accurately identifying anomalies in the ICS data. The associated code can be accessed via a GitHub repository. When dealing with a random sample of size n from a distribution of unknown parameter σ, which can be broken down into two parts: a parameter μ and a mixing distribution π, we are tasked with estimating the expected value of σ. This is a crucial problem in various fields, such as biology and engineering, where σ represents quantities like the size of particles or the duration of events. This is supported by a region surrounding the gap where CO is present, but C$^{16}$O and C$^{18}$O are depleted, suggesting that CO is formed through chemical reactions when the gas surface density drops below a certain threshold. Achieving consistency in image content is crucial for achieving visually appealing results. Current methods for achieving this are limited in their ability to model relationships between image regions and often require complex annotations. In response, we introduce VICTOR, a model that uses a dual transformer architecture to identify inconsistencies in images. The model's first transformer is pre-trained using a novel task of contrasting image components, while its second transformer is fine-tuned for incompatibility detection using a simplified form of annotation. When evaluated on the Fashion Incompatibility dataset, VICTOR outperforms previous state-of-the-art models by a significant margin of 10.5%. Additionally, we demonstrate the benefits of our pre-training task by comparing the performance of VICTOR and a model without pre-training. VICTOR's source code will be made available.

Knowledge graph embeddings have achieved remarkable success in link prediction, but their application to temporal knowledge graphs remains subpar when compared to model-independent methods. This disparity is attributed to the fact that most existing embedding models are designed for static graphs and fail to effectively incorporate time-annotated quadruples. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel approach that utilizes static models in a more effective manner. Specifically, we develop a method that transforms temporal quadruples into a series of corresponding static triples, allowing for the utilization of a single static model. Furthermore, we introduce a simple yet efficient way to transform temporal quadruples into static triples, outperforming existing approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses model-specific and model-agnostic techniques in link prediction tasks. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the impact of our quadruple transformation method. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengwenwen/TKEP.

This study focuses on visually guided sound synthesis through conditional waveform
generation. The goal is to create a model that can produce high-quality sounds in
response to visual cues. The key challenge lies in the diverse range of sounds that
can be generated, making it difficult to create a model that can produce high-quality
sounds consistently. To overcome this issue, we developed a WaveNet-based model that
can produce high-quality sounds at a high temporal resolution. The model's efficacy
is evaluated using a dataset of visually guided sound clips. The results show that the
model can synthesize sounds that are similar to those in the training dataset, as
verified through subjective testing. The model's performance is further improved by
incorporating audio cycle-consistency loss and spectral features in the discriminator. 
The work presented here represents a significant advancement in the field of visually
guided sound synthesis. The associated audio-visual samples can be found at
https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/audiogen/. The code has been made available on
github.com/audigen/visual_sound_synthesis.

In machine learning, data debugging is the process of identifying and correcting issues with training datasets. Our approach uses the Shapley value framework to quantify the contribution of each data preprocessing step in an end-to-end machine learning pipeline. We develop a plug-and-play method for calculating Shapley values in a distributed pipeline and demonstrate its effectiveness with two plug-and-play implementations: one general method and another tailored to image classification tasks. Experimental results on multiple datasets and pipeline components confirm the accuracy and efficiency of our approach. Additionally, our method facilitates cost-sensitive data debugging by allocating budget to the most important preprocessing steps. Our findings show that improving our base model using budget-constrained data debugging yields better performance than optimizing the base model alone. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are often limited by the coherence time, which is inversely proportional to the electron bunch length.  We present a modified chirp-taper scheme that enables the reduction of pulse duration below the coherence time by shortening the bunch afterpulse.  This is achieved through a reduction in the radiating charge, which in turn requires a higher radiator field to sustain oscillations.  We demonstrate the potential for generating attosecond pulses in the XUV and soft X-ray range using the LCLS, FERMI, and SARAF facilities, assuming optimized undulator systems and inelasticity parameters.  Specifically, our model predicts the attainment of $200\, \mathrm{as}$ FWHM pulses at $10\, \mathrm{eV}$ for LCLS and $20\, \mathrm{as}$ at $5\, \mathrm{eV}$ for FERMI, all within a relatively small modification of the tapering field.  Furthermore, our simulations indicate that SARAF can produce $100\, \mathrm{fs}$ pulses in the soft X-ray range with a relatively small undulator system modification.  We anticipate that this scheme will significantly contribute to the development of attosecond pulse generation in XUV and soft X-ray FELs.

Election manipulation through the alteration of election district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing threat to democratic integrity.  We present a method for detecting
this form of election manipulation by comparing the outcomes of simulated annealing
algorithms with and without intervention in the district boundaries.  Our approach
utilizes a model that can be applied to various types of election manipulation with
minimal modification.  We test this method in the context of North Carolina's 1st
congressional district, where it indicates significant evidence of manipulation in
the state's 1st congressional district in the 2016 elections.  We also demonstrate
that our method can be used to identify the extent of manipulation that would be
detected through statistical analysis.  Furthermore, we show that our method can be
applied to detect manipulation in local elections.  We make our code available for
public use.

This research introduces a novel multivariate spatial model designed to analyze extreme events in the ocean by considering the relationships between multiple locations and variables. The model relies on a joint extreme value distribution derived from spatial extreme value processes, and incorporates a Markov random field to capture positive and negative dependencies between locations. Parameter estimation is achieved through a maximum likelihood approach, and the model's performance is demonstrated in a case study of extreme wave heights in the North Atlantic. The results show significant improvements in the model's ability to capture extreme event relationships and spatial correlations when compared to a simpler model. The developed methodology can be applied to various ocean applications, and the code is available in an open-source package.

A key concept in robotics called manipulability is downplayed in its suitability for tasks that require learning due to its non-Euclidean nature and variable scale. This research presents innovative methods to address these limitations, enabling the efficient transfer of learning across different robot manipulator configurations within the manipulability domain. Firstly, we develop a straightforward algorithm to align the manipulability domains of source and target robots using parallel transport. Secondly, we enhance the traditional Iterative Closest Point algorithm to account for the curved manifold structure of manipulability, resulting in a more robust and efficient correspondence computation. This improved correspondence enables the transfer of key target manipulator features, such as points and trajectories. The proposed approach is validated through successful experiments involving various robot manipulator configurations, including 6-DoF serial and 7-DoF parallel designs. The results demonstrate successful transfers of target features to the source manipulator's domain, with the enhanced ICPT outperforming the basic PT method in accuracy. We introduce a novel framework to learn the three-dimensional pose of a object through visual observations of it rotating. This approach is inspired by real-world scenarios where objects are often placed on turntables for precise 3D reconstruction. Our framework, known as Accidental Turntables, can learn to predict 3D pose from a single image by leveraging a dataset of objects rotating in 3D, regardless of the specific viewpoint or orientation. This is achieved by modeling a function that maps pose to viewpoint, allowing for accurate predictions in novel scenarios. Our method excels in 3D pose prediction and view synthesis tasks, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we created the Carla Turntable Dataset, a large collection of autonomous car images featuring turntables with diverse objects, viewpoints, and poses. This dataset serves as the foundation for our method and will be open-sourced to benefit the research community. The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the significance of reliable public health information. Social media platforms like Twitter have become hubs for disseminating both fact-based and false information, influencing users' perceptions. To mitigate the spread of misinformation, it is crucial to create systems that can differentiate between adopted and rejected information on Twitter. This task is complex due to the varying quality of available tweets and labels. In this study, we introduce a novel framework that leverages BERT to identify whether a retweet indicates the adoption or rejection of misinformation. Our framework's performance surpasses that of baseline models, which rely on tweet content or user behavior. Additionally, we provide a refined corpus with high-quality labels and evaluate our model's robustness to data imperfections. Our model code and data are available for public access.

However, the security of these applications is compromised by vulnerabilities in their code, often stemming from dependencies installed through package managers. This research introduces EVKGC, a graph-based knowledge construction method for vulnerability information in software dependencies. We also demonstrate how vulnerability dissemination can be predicted using graph algorithms, with the Cargo ecosystem exhibiting distinct propagation patterns compared to other ecosystems. Cerius, a Very Forward Hadron Spectrometer, is currently under development to be part of the LHCUpgrade and FAIR experiments, as well as a detector for the Cosmic Ray Observatory at the Pierre Auger Center. Cerius will be situated at zero coverage with the ability to detect hadrons down to 1 GeV/c directly in the center of mass system. Its innovative design features will be discussed, including the use of a tungsten-scintillator calorimeter to identify the mass of hadrons and a silicon tracker at the front to determine their momentum. This hybrid approach will provide in-depth analysis of the mass and rapidity of hadrons, expanding our understanding of the production mechanisms of light hadrons in the range of 10 to 300 GeV/c. Additionally, this detector will significantly enhance the detection capabilities of the Pierre Auger Observatory, allowing for more precise analysis of the composition of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. Furthermore, its ability to detect the products of charm and beauty quarks will provide valuable insights into their interaction with the cosmic ray shower. Lastly, this detector will significantly contribute to the detection of charm and beauty quarks produced in the forward direction in LHC and FAIR experiments, offering new perspectives on their properties and production mechanisms. This talk will provide a comprehensive overview of the design, goals, and potential applications of Cerius.

Deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) are designed to process 2D image data, but they treat pixels as scalar values, overlooking valuable orientation information present in images. This research introduces Orientation Convolutional Networks (OCNs), a novel DCNN architecture that incorporates orientation context, enhancing the representation of local image features. By incorporating a new orientation convolution layer, OCNs can learn and differentiate various images that share similar content but differ in orientation. This is achieved by integrating a circular kernel bank, with each kernel optimized to capture specific orientation features. The innovative architecture of OCNs allows them to outperform conventional DCNNs in orientation recognition and image classification tasks, while significantly reducing the computational burden through kernel bank sharing. Experimental results demonstrate the potential of OCNs to improve local feature representation. The code will be publicly available.

The Graph Convolutional Network has shown remarkable potential in point cloud processing. However, traditional GCN's efficiency is compromised due to its high computational complexity and extensive memory requirements. This study addresses these issues by introducing an optimized GCN architecture, tailored for point cloud applications. We substitute the conventional multi-layer perceptron in GCN with a Laplace kernel-based fully connected layer, reducing the complexity of graph convolution from O(N^2) to O(N). Furthermore, we substitute the expensive matrix multiplication in graph convolution with an average pooling method, reducing the complexity from O(N^2) to O(N). Experimental results demonstrate that our optimized GCN significantly outperforms the standard GCN, achieving a substantial runtime boost of up to 7.9 times. This optimized GCN achieves state-of-the-art performance in point cloud semantic segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuke2020/EGCN.

Deep neural networks are vulnerable to 'backdoors,' which can be triggered in the model's predictions by specific inputs. Most existing backdoor attacks rely on host inputs embedded in the model during training, limiting our understanding of neural behavior. In this research, we develop a new type of backdoor attack that doesn't rely on host inputs, which can be triggered by inputs unrelated to the model's host data. We also introduce a semantic backdoor attack, where the model is manipulated to produce specific output labels based on target input words. The model's host data is bypassed in both scenarios, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our attacks by successfully triggering them in models not exposed to the backdoor during training. We also show that detecting these types of backdoor attacks is extremely challenging. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/chenyong2005/SHTG.

This research paper delves into the chemical makeup of stars that harbor terrestrial planets similar to Earth. The Skincare project is an interactive AI-powered system designed to aid in the differential diagnosis of skin cancers by utilizing deep learning and image annotation. Developed to mimic a dermatologist's decision-making process, the system incorporates multiple models that work in tandem to identify areas of suspicion and gather additional annotations from users to fine-tune its diagnoses. Comprised of an image classification model and an interactive segmentation module, the Skincare system was tested on a dataset of 15,278 images and achieved notable results, outperforming general dermatologists in lesion type classification and producing accurate diagnoses with a limited number of user annotations. Furthermore, the system's ability to engage users through real-time feedback and identify critical diagnostic regions has significant implications for the development of dermatological decision support tools. By integrating the Skincare system into clinical practice, the accuracy of dermatologist diagnoses can be enhanced, and the decision-making process can be streamlined. Additionally, the system's open-source framework and annotated dataset can facilitate research and development in dermatology. This study examines how the emergence of novel investment strategies affects the performance of established ones within a stylized financial market model. Our analysis reveals that the impact of new strategies on old ones' returns can be both positive and negative. We identify two key conditions that influence this effect: the new strategy's profitability and similarity to existing ones. A profitable new strategy is likely to reduce the returns of similar old strategies, while one with little similarity may boost the returns of old strategies that employ a different investment approach. Our findings are consistent across different market settings, including cases with high and variable liquidity. Furthermore, our results suggest that the reduction in returns of old strategies resulting from the introduction of new ones could be substantial, lasting for an extended period. To mitigate this effect, financial market regulators may consider implementing policies to reduce the concentration of investor portfolios in specific assets. Federated learning has shown great potential for decentralized training on private client data. In this research, we address the challenge of audiosignal classification, specifically noise recognition, by a group of devices with access to the same classes but not each other's data. To enhance robustness against various types of noise, we develop a zero-shot federated learning framework that integrates domain adaptation and representation learning. We test this approach with two widely used datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in a scenario with four unknown classes and noisy labels. Our results show that this technique outperforms traditional FL and domain adaptation methods, achieving a significant improvement of 15% or higher in accuracy. We introduce xor filters, a new family of approximate membership filters, outperforming both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in speed and space efficiency. Our membership filters utilize a combination of xor hash and bit xor operations to determine membership, achieving significantly faster lookup times and reduced storage requirements. A Bloom filter is a prerequisite for an xor filter, and we demonstrate that an xor filter can be constructed by replacing each modulo operation in a Bloom filter hash function with an xor operation, resulting in an xor filter with equivalent performance but reduced storage needs. An alternative method for creating an xor filter involves using a hash function that produces xor values, and we show that such hash functions can be designed efficiently. Furthermore, we present a new type of xor filter, called the xor filter with correction, which offers a trade-off between storage utilization and false positive rate. Our experimental results confirm that xor filters outperform Bloom and Cuckoo filters in both space efficiency and search speed. For example, an xor filter can reduce storage requirements by 50% and accelerate search times by up to 30x compared to a Bloom filter with similar false positive rates. Additionally, xor filters can be used to develop more efficient approximate set covers algorithms, and we present a heuristic approach that yields a 20% reduction in computation time and up to 5x reduction in memory usage compared to existing algorithms. Our xor filter implementation is available as open-source software. A detailed tutorial on designing xor hash functions is also provided. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of 13 different Bloom filter variants, and our results show that a recently proposed filter, called the Bloomier filter, exhibits poor performance and is best avoided. Our research also reveals that another filter, called the static keyed Bloom filter, performs poorly in environments with frequent insertions, and we recommend an alternative, called the dynamic static keyed Bloom filter. Our research also reveals that another filter, called the Cuckoo filter with eviction, performs poorly in environments with frequent lookups, and we recommend an alternative, called the dynamic Cuckoo filter. transaction data, drawing on the On The Money Tree algorithm. It assesses the
trend prediction capabilities of this algorithm in comparison to Random Walk
hypothesis using historical S&P 500 trade records. Results show that this
approach yields significant positive returns in backtesting scenarios. To mitigate
overfitting, the algorithm's performance is evaluated on out-of-sample trade
sequences. Furthermore, the study explores the impact of the length of the
transaction history on its predictive accuracy. It also examines the potential
of this method to forecast future market trends. To validate the approach, a
statistical analysis is performed to identify the trend patterns in the trade
data. This analysis reveals that the results are not merely a product of chance. 
Finally, the study's findings are compared to those of a leading technical
analysis tool, TradingView. It appears that the trend patterns identified by
this method are distinct from those reported by TradingView. This approach may
offer a valuable alternative to traditional technical analysis methods.

As mobile devices generate an enormous amount of data, federated learning has emerged as a promising approach to train machine learning models while maintaining data privacy. However, the potential abuse of sensitive information and the presence of malicious clients pose significant threats to the FL process. In this paper, we introduce FLVoogd, a refined federated learning framework that balances data security and system reliability. Specifically, FLVoogd incorporates Byzantine fault tolerance and differential privacy to safeguard sensitive information and prevent malicious attacks, respectively. We then propose an adaptive learning rate scheduling technique to enhance robustness and demonstrate the effectiveness of FLVoogd through comprehensive experiments. Furthermore, we open-source FLVoogd to facilitate future research and development.

The transfer of learning algorithms from simulated environments to the real world is known as Sim2Real. Our research focuses on the development of a Sim2Real approach for autonomous driving, which is a complex task. The aim is to train a single model to predict control actions both in simulated and real-world contexts. The challenge lies in the disparity between simulated and real-world images, which can be attributed to various factors such as lighting conditions, road obstacles, and the presence of vehicles. To bridge this gap, we propose utilizing image gradients as a bridge for transfer learning. The gradient structure allows low-level features to be transferred while high-level features are learned afresh. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through autonomous driving experiments conducted in both simulated and real-world settings. The results indicate significant performance enhancements over state-of-the-art Sim2Real methods. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepDriveIT/Sim2Real.

Unrestricted media, encompassing a broad range of content types including images and videos, is becoming increasingly vulnerable to deepfakes. This research addresses the deepfake detection challenge on non-sequential, unrestricted media by introducing the DeepAll task. DeepAll requires participants to classify individual samples as genuine or deepfake. Our analysis of the DeepAll dataset reveals that deepfakes pose a significant threat, with over 99% of samples confirming the presence of forgery. We introduce an advanced deepfake detection model, DRU, featuring self-similar blocks and a self-attention mechanism. Comparative evaluations on the DeepAll dataset demonstrate the exceptional performance of DRU against leading detection models. Furthermore, we establish new detection benchmarks on the DeepAll dataset. The DeepAll dataset and challenge are now accessible at https://unrestricted-deepfake-detection-challenge.com/. This study is a submission to the ICCV 2021 DeepAll challenge.

In complex systems with numerous sensors and variables, operational data is often partially observable due to missing values, making it difficult to detect changes and isolate their sources. Current methods either ignore the missing values or require a significant amount of pre-collected data to create a complete historical record. We present a new approach that adaptively handles partially-observable data streams from multiple sources, allowing for the timely and accurate identification of system changes and their causes. Our method integrates three key components: handling missing values, monitoring and isolating changes, all of which are highly efficient and adaptable. We demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments involving a real-world industrial control system. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of its performance and a framework for selecting critical variables to improve performance. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

A significant roadblock in developing effective document extraction models lies in the labor-intensive process of obtaining labeled data. Our research presents a novel, efficient approach to label documents semi-supervisely by leveraging a weakly-supervised text extraction task that only requires batch-level annotations. We introduce a simple yet effective model that can accurately identify dominant text regions without the need for exhaustive bounding box labeling. Our model outperforms existing semi-supervised methods by achieving a 3% improvement in extraction accuracy on the Table Extraction dataset, and demonstrates comparable results on the LayoutText dataset. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset, SemiSupDoc, which consists of 200 pages with batch-level annotations and serves as a benchmark for evaluating semi-supervised document processing tasks. The code and dataset are publicly available on GitHub.

We present a new algorithm for solving constrained Markov decision processes, which employs a primal-dual method by integrating the value iteration algorithm with dual ascent. This approach yields a straightforward and efficient scheme that converges to an optimal solution with little computational expense. Furthermore, we establish a critical condition under which the generated sequence will asymptotically converge to the optimal solution only if the value function sequence converges. We test this method in a range of scenarios, which demonstrate its computational efficiency and scalability. Notably, we show that this method can be used to solve a challenging control problem with a computational time savings of almost two orders of magnitude compared to prior techniques.
