Actor-critic reinforcement learning has achieved significant success in various robotic tasks. However, its policy network often necessitates a large number of samples for accurate estimation, which can lead to excessive overfitting and hinder training. This paper proposes a novel actor-critic framework that integrates the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method to boost sample efficiency and prevent overfitting. By leveraging the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method, the policy network learns to concentrate its distribution on high-probability actions based on past experiences. This is accomplished through the calculation of the natural gradient of the policy network's Hamiltonian, which is then incorporated into the actor-critic framework. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses the standard actor-critic framework in terms of both sample efficiency and robustness to overfitting. Additionally, the method exhibits superior performance in inverting geometric transformations and completing maze tasks. The method's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuc/hmc_actor_critic.

This paper outlines a multi-layer navigation control system that integrates sonar and wheel speed sensors on an autonomous mobile robot. The mid-level module adjusts the path in real-time to avoid collisions using a Sonar Fusion-based obstacle detection system. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) is a complex task that becomes even more challenging when it comes to low-resource and composed languages, which involve multiple scripts or languages mixed into one. Existing approaches often require a substantial amount of labeled data to achieve good performance. However, obtaining such a dataset is impractical due to the time-consuming process of transcription. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method that generates synthetic training data in an unsupervised and compositional manner. This approach leverages pre-trained models and a simple yet effective encoder-decoder model to create realistic datasets. To evaluate our approach, we created synthetic datasets for two low-resource handwritten datasets, HTRDB-Compo, which consists of composed English-Arabic and English-Roman text. The results show that our method significantly improves the performance of the models when tested on the HTRDB challenge benchmark. Notably, our approach outperforms the baseline model by 10-20% in character error rate. The source code and synthetic datasets are available on GitHub for reproducibility.

We introduce a dynamic learning process centered on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model, which serves as a gateway to understanding topological concepts. The SSH model is brought to life through a hands-on, interactive simulation, allowing learners to discover its topological characteristics by exploring the real-space properties of the pseudospin. A guided journey is provided, guiding students to discover the following concepts: (1) the connection between pseudospin orientation and energy gaps; (2) topological characteristics from real and imaginary components of pseudospin; (3) the relationship between sublattice imbalances and energy spectra; (extended SSH models); and (the impact of mid-gap states in extended SSH models). This curriculum is designed to be adaptable for both undergraduate and graduate levels, allowing for adjustments based on the audience's prior knowledge of topological concepts. Additionally, the accompanying software and educational materials can be accessed through a public repository. Furthermore, a comprehensive set of assessment tools is offered to gauge students' understanding of the concepts presented in this curriculum. This approach enables the solution of larger-scale problems, and we highlight its benefits through additional numerical experiments. Ultimately, we contribute a general framework for constructing Nash equilibria through mixed-integer nonlinear programming, and we demonstrate its efficacy through a comprehensive set of numerical results. This research introduces a novel text-conditioned image creation method that leverages a stable diffusion model, allowing for the generation of images that accurately reflect the provided semantic guidance. Unlike existing text-conditioning techniques that focus on the input sequence, this model's language conditioner is trained to produce a stable latent space representation that is less prone to variability. A novel approach to reversible steganography is introduced in this research, employing Bayesian Neural Networks to enhance the quality of coverting and recovering data. The BNN framework is characterized by its predictive distributions - predictive means are utilized for data conversion, while predictive variance is utilized as an embedding probability. To optimize BNN performance, a regression analysis based on the Wasserstein distance is developed. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed BNN method surpasses existing reversible steganography techniques in terms of data quality and embedding capacity. Additionally, this method maintains exceptional recovery performance. A comprehensive examination of the statistical properties of BNN predictions is included in the supplementary materials. The research code and additional materials are available for public access at the specified URL.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal patterns, but the relationship between these modes remains unclear. We investigated this question by analyzing minimal videos - short clips that humans can recognize, but deep neural networks struggle. These minimal videos are composed of either spatial or motion components that humans use for recognition. Interestingly, we found that they are not simply sequential or combined with static patterns, but rather, humans integrate them using temporal relationships. We also found that these spatial and motion components are not interchangeable, and we explored how they are processed in the human visual system. Additionally, we demonstrated that deep neural networks can learn to recognize these minimal videos with only minimal adjustments to the architecture. This new model, called Dyn-Net, integrates spatial and motion patterns through temporal relationships, and it significantly improves performance on several challenging dynamic recognition tasks. We further validated the importance of these temporal relationships by conducting human vision experiments, showing that recognition is impaired when these relationships are distorted. Our findings provide new insights into how humans recognize patterns and can serve as a guide for designing more effective deep neural networks. A video showcasing the minimal videos is available on YouTube at https://youtu.be/6Qh6Qe4Z4Qo. This work is based on the authors' previous study, which introduced the concept of minimal videos (Nearney et al., 2020). The current research extends this study, exploring the composition of these minimal videos and designing Dyn-Net to surpass the performance of deep neural networks on dynamic recognition tasks. features human body expressions in various poses and viewpoints. Comprising
over 1.1 million images from 16 different viewpoints, HUMBI also includes
precise 3D annotations for 250,000 frames. Our aim is to enhance the accuracy
of human pose estimation in 3D space by addressing the challenges posed by
limited viewpoints and incomplete 3D data. A new benchmark challenge, the HUMBI

estimation. The winning models are evaluated on the HUMBI dataset and our
pretrained 2D/3D pose estimation methods are also showcased. The HUMBI dataset and

We introduce a task representation learning approach that uses neural networks to capture essential information from the source language. This paper introduces the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model, a neural network that generates raw audio signals using an autoregressive approach. It incorporates pitch-dependent dilated convolutional layers and a pitch extraction module to improve WaveNet's efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model achieves comparable high-quality audio synthesis performance to WaveNet, while reducing the number of parameters by approximately 50%. The model's source code will be publicly available.

Recommender Systems that are interactive have to cope with the dual challenges of
sparse and subjective user preference data. This research presents a novel CF method
that leverages biclustering to address these issues. The proposed approach groups
users and items in a way that enhances generalization while preserving individual
variations. It achieves this through the simultaneous optimization of user and item
clusters based on the overall and per-group preference matrices. Experimental
results demonstrate that the model outperforms state-of-the-art CF methods by a
significant margin on three diverse datasets. Moreover, the framework's ability to
capture fine-grained user preferences enables the successful integration of session-
based CF techniques. This yields substantial improvements of 6.4% and 11.9% in
predictive accuracy when combined with a basic CF and the state-of-the-art CF method,
respectively. The model's effectiveness and transparent recommendations of user
sub-groups with similar preferences are also showcased. The source code is openly
available for reproduction of the study's findings.

Existing neural style transfer methods primarily focus on maintaining the original image's semantic structure while incorporating the teacher image's style. However, they typically discard this structure in their inverse model, which is unsuitable for real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose a novel two-stage framework that distills the teacher's style from paired images. Our method first extracts local features from paired images and generates global style parameters through a clustering process. These parameters are then utilized to develop a robust style transfer algorithm and its corresponding inverse model. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in preserving the original image's structure and facilitating robust color grading applications. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyin95/Distill-Style-Transfer.

We introduce a new approach to autonomous robot navigation that combines elements of active inference and deep neural networks. Active inference models agents as making decisions to reduce uncertainty in their environment through informed actions. We apply this framework to a simple robot navigation task using a deep neural network to model the agent's beliefs about the environment. Our results show that this method produces efficient and goal-directed behavior in the robot. We also examine the benefits of incorporating the active inference framework into a deep neural network, compared to a standard goal-orientated agent. compared to existing estimates using waveform fitting. Additionally, this work

residual eccentricity to influence spin estimates, but concludes that this is likely

Event identification in graph structures can be crucial for real-world applications such as network security and urban planning analysis. Most current approaches, however, focus solely on static graphs, neglecting the importance of dynamic graphs. To address this, we introduce a new task known as Event Detection on Dynamic Graphs (EDDG), which aims to identify emerging events within a temporal graph represented by a series of snapshots. To tackle EDDG, we propose a framework that combines a node feature extractor, an event representation learner, and an event classifier. To evaluate our framework, we create a dataset consisting of 11,000 graphs and manually label the events within. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which significantly outperforms baseline methods by 10-20%. The source code and dataset are available on GitHub for reproducibility.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and accountability in such systems are achieved by reducing the complexity of their inner workings, yet this simplification may not always accurately reflect their true nature. In this paper, we explore the link between explainable AI and software requirements engineering, focusing on how requirements can facilitate honest and simplified understanding of AI models. We propose a two-part approach: first, classifying the XAI challenge and proposed solutions; second, outlining a comprehensive methodology for deriving explainability requirements from stakeholder needs. This methodology is exemplified in a case study on a digital assistant. This study's outcomes and future research directions are also discussed.

Conversely, when the embedded PIC component spans across multiple islands, it successfully captures the island coalescence phenomenon. These findings are consistent with full PIC simulation results. Consequently, MHD-AEPIC emerges as a viable and efficient tool for studying magnetic reconnection processes. Its potential applications include investigating reconnection in various astrophysical and space plasma environments.
